title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarking Suite, Release Notes, Known Issues, and Runbooks
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary
This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling strategy, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite guidance, recent release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks for Redwood Inference's serving runtime. It is intended for engineers on the serving-runtime, infra, and SRE teams and is the canonical reference for diagnosing performance regressions, planning capacity, and running controlled rollouts.

Table of contents
1. Overview and goals
2. Runtime architecture (components & data flows)
3. Kernel and scheduling design
4. Profiling & performance playbook
5. Benchmarking suite and test recipes
6. Release notes & compatibility matrix (last 3 releases)
7. Known issues and mitigations
8. Runbooks: incidents, scaling, and rollouts
9. Team wiki links and ownership
10. Appendix: key configs and commands

1. Overview and goals
- Primary goals: predictable P99 latency, high aggregated throughput, graceful degradation under overload, and transparent unit economics.
- Production SLOs (global):
  - Generation API (<=128 tokens): P50 < 40ms, P95 < 80ms, P99 < 120ms.
  - Chat API (context up to 2048 tokens): P95 < 200ms, P99 < 400ms.
  - Embedding API: P95 < 60ms, P99 < 150ms.
- Operational targets: paging threshold = SLO breach lasting >= 5m with error rate > 1%.

2. Runtime architecture (components & data flows)
- Key services and components:
  - frontdoor-api: REST gateway for client requests, auth, and routing.
  - router-service: policy-based request router (region, tier, model variant).
  - scheduler: request batching and GPU assignment service (per-pool).
  - worker (inference-agent): hosts model runtime, manages KV cache and kernels.
  - cache-service (optional): central prefix/KV cache for warm starts across workers.
  - metrics-collector: aggregates latency, KV hit/miss, utilization, and tail stats.
- Data flow (high level):
  1. frontdoor-api validates and forwards to router-service.
  2. router-service applies policy and selects a pool + model variant.
  3. scheduler groups compatible requests into batches (continuous batching) and assigns a worker.
  4. worker loads model weights (if not resident), consults KV cache, executes kernels, streams tokens back to frontdoor.
  5. metrics-collector records per-token and per-request metrics; rollups feed into Console dashboards.
- Deployment topology notes:
  - Dedicated pools and private deployments use the same code paths; differences are config-only.
  - Workers can be pinned to GPU types; scheduler uses hardware tags to select kernel code paths.

3. Kernel and scheduling design
- Kernel selection:
  - At model load time the worker probes GPU capability (cuda compute capability, memory bandwidth) and chooses a kernel set (fast-matmul, fused-attn, quantized-kernels).
  - Kernel set metadata includes supported sequence lengths, batch alignment constraints, and expected per-token throughput.
- Scheduling strategy:
  - Continuous batching: scheduler maintains per-model queues and emits batches when one of three conditions is met: (1) max_batch_size reached, (2) batching_timeout (default 8ms) elapsed, or (3) latency budget remaining for the request forces immediate flush.
  - Work-packing: small requests are packed into larger kernels to amortize kernel launch overhead. The scheduler prefers same-sequence-length packing to minimize padding.
  - KV cache affinity: requests that share conversation keys are affinity-scheduled to workers that have a warm KV cache to reduce cold-start token costs.
  - Preemption: long-running requests (streaming with >1024 tokens) are deprioritized when queue depth exceeds overload_threshold (default 80% utilization).
- Resource accounting:
  - Per-worker GPU reservation tracks active tokens-in-flight and estimated token-cost per kernel. The scheduler ensures headroom for high-priority traffic (reserved 10% by default).

4. Profiling & performance playbook
- When to profile:
  - New model onboarding, after kernel changes, after driver or CUDA upgrades, or when P95/P99 latencies increase by >20% for a sustained 15m window.
- Tools and instrumentation:
  - rwd-prof: internal profiler that collects NVTX spans, kernel durations, memory copies, and per-op breakdowns.
  - metrics-collector / Grafana: request-level histograms, token-level cost, KV hit/miss, throttle counts.
  - perfkit: flamegraph generation from stack samples.
- Profiling steps:
  1. Reproduce in staging using the profiling harness: rwdctl profile start --target pool=<pool> --qps <baseline> --duration 10m --model <model>.
  2. Collect rwd-prof output, kernel timelines, and NVTX.
  3. Generate breakdown: time in kernel (%.), memcpy (%.), scheduler delay (ms), queue wait (ms), and idle time.
  4. If kernel time dominates, run A/B with kernel variants: fast-matmul vs quantized-kernels.
  5. If memcopy dominates, check pinned-memory settings and interconnect topology (PCIe vs NVLink).
  6. Validate with microbenchmarks in the benchmarking suite (see section 5).
- Quick checks (first 10 minutes):
  - KV hit ratio < 30%? Re-evaluate affinity scheduling and warm-up policy.
  - Batch sizes frequently < 30% of max_batch_size? Lower batching_timeout or adjust frontdoor routing to coalesce similar requests.
  - GPU active utilization < 40% at expected QPS? Investigate kernel selection and memcopy bottlenecks.

5. Benchmarking suite and test recipes
- Purpose: validate per-kernel throughput, end-to-end P99 under realistic request distributions, and compare quantized vs full-precision for unit economics.
- Components:
  - microbench: measures single-kernel and single-layer throughput and memory usage.
  - qpsbench: generates traffic shapes (spiky, uniform, conversational) and measures request-level latencies and tail.
  - eval-harness: runs quality regressions for quantized kernels to ensure output fidelity within thresholds.
- Example test recipes:
  - Microkernel throughput: microbench run --model <model> --seq 512 --batch 8 --iters 200 --kernels [fast-matmul, fused-attn]. Record avg and std.
  - E2E P99 under mixed traffic: qpsbench --shape conversational --users 2000 --qps 400 --duration 20m --model <model> --kv-warmup 30%.
  - Quantization regression: eval-harness run --model <model_fp32> --quant <config> --prompt-set /prompt-sets/corda-collection-2029.json --threshold 95% similarity.
- Performance targets for benchmarks (example):
  - microkernel: 1.8x higher throughput using fused-attn vs baseline on A100-80GB for seq=1024.
  - E2E: P99 within 1.2x of baseline while reducing per-token GPU time by >=20% using quantized-kernels.

6. Release notes & compatibility matrix (last 3 releases)
- 2029-06-10 (v8.4.0):
  - Kernel improvements: added int8 quantized-kernels for transformer FFN that reduce token compute by ~22% for tested workloads.
  - Scheduler: adaptive batching_timeout introduced (trial, default enabled for experimental pools).
  - Backwards-incompatible change: quantized-kernel ABI 2.0 — models must be re-quantized with rwd-quant v3.
- 2029-04-02 (v8.3.1):
  - Stability: fixed race condition in worker cache eviction.
  - Observability: added per-kernel histograms to metrics-collector.
- 2029-01-12 (v8.2.0):
  - Feature: KV cache affinity scheduling and warm-up API.
  - Performance: improved fused-attn launch path for sequence lengths <128.
- Upgrade guidance:
  - Use canary pool for 48h with qpsbench simulated traffic before broad rollout.
  - Run eval-harness with production prompt sets to ensure quality preserved for quantized paths.

7. Known issues and mitigations (active)
- Issue: Sporadic P99 spikes after driver 535.x upgrade on some A100 fleets.
  - Symptoms: P99 increases by 2-4x, kernel durations show variance spikes, memcpy latencies stable.
  - Mitigation: Roll back driver to 530.x, enable conservative kernel set (fallback to baseline), and open ticket with HW partner.
  - Owner: gpu-fleet-and-capacity team.
- Issue: KV cache thrash when many short conversations with large state are served on a small worker pool.
  - Mitigation: Increase cache size per-worker, enable LRU tiering, or route long state conversations to dedicated pools.
  - Owner: eng-serving-runtime.
- Issue: Quantized-kernel mismatch for rare layernorm edge-case leading to degraded output on a subset of prompts.
  - Mitigation: Add prompt-set to regression suite and pin affected models to FP32 variant until fix released.
  - Owner: applied-ml-and-evals.

8. Runbooks: incidents, scaling, and rollouts
- Incident: sustained P99 SLO breach (>=15m)
  1. Triage in #oncall-serving channel. Attach Grafana dashboard (ServingRuntime / Latency / P99).
  2. Run quick checks: rwdctl health check pool=<affected_pool> and rwdctl metrics tail --since 30m --filter p99.
  3. If kernel durations high: scale up workers (rwdctl pool scale --pool <pool> --delta +2) and enable conservative kernel set: rwdctl config set --pool <pool> kernel_set=baseline.
  4. If memcopy high: check node-level IO metrics and network; consider rolling restart of affected nodes.
  5. If KV-miss spike: temporarily disable affinity to reduce hot eviction: rwdctl config set --pool <pool> kv_affinity=false.
  6. Escalate to infra oncall if node-level GPU errors or driver alerts present.
  7. Post-incident: open postmortem using template /templates/incident-postmortem and attach profiling outputs.
- Scaling up pool (capacity planning)
  1. Validate QPS and token-distribution via metrics-collector reports for the last 7 days.
  2. Use capacity planner (internal) with input: target_qps, p95_target, avg_tokens_per_request.
  3. Reserve nodes and apply config: rwdctl pool create --name <pool> --gpu_type A100-80GB --replicas <n>.
  4. Run qpsbench smoke test.
- Canary rollout for kernel change
  1. Create experimental pool with kernel_set=quantized-v2 and route 2% of traffic.
  2. Run qpsbench with production shape for 72h and monitor P99, KV hit ratio, and quality alerts.
  3. If regressions < threshold, incrementally increase traffic (2% -> 10% -> 30% -> 100%).
  4. If quality alerts trigger, rollback routing and mark the build as blocked in the release tracker.

9. Team wiki links and ownership
- Owners and escalation paths:
  - eng-serving-runtime: primary owner for runtime code, scheduler, and worker implementation (oncall rota in PagerDuty team: serving-runtime).
  - eng-infra / gpu-fleet-and-capacity: hardware, drivers, and node provisioning.
  - applied-ml-and-evals: quantization, evals, and downstream quality checks.
  - eng-sre: SLOs, incident postmortems, and runbook audits.
- Useful pages (internal):

10. Appendix: key configs and commands
- Example config snippet (pool defaults):
  - max_batch_size: 64
  - batching_timeout_ms: 8
  - kv_cache_size_mb: 8192
  - reserved_headroom_pct: 10
  - kernel_set: baseline
- Common commands:
  - Start profiling: rwdctl profile start --pool <pool> --model <model> --duration 10m --out /tmp/profile.json
  - Run microbench: microbench --model <model> --seq 512 --batch 8 --iters 200
  - Scale pool: rwdctl pool scale --pool <pool> --delta +3
  - Canary traffic route: rwdctl route update --from frontdoor --to pool=<canary_pool> --weight 2%
